title: When Is a Cheap Fairness Edit Safe? Screening Post-Hoc Edits in Two-Sided Matching Markets

paper.title:
When Is a Cheap Fairness Edit Safe? Screening Post-Hoc Edits in
Two-Sided Matching Markets
paper.abstract:
Abstract Two-sided matching systems, such as admissions pipelines, allocate
opportunities jointly. Reducing a protected attribute’s influence usually
requires encoder retraining. We study a closed-form linear projector that
does this at inference time. For markets that stay vertically ordered before
and after the edit, we bound the mean welfare change by the edit-induced
appeal shift and an explicit remainder. A probabilistic refinement replaces
worst-case constants with a data-dependent deviation term. A pre-deployment
screen combines a verticality test with a welfare sweep and returns PASS,
KILL, or OUT-OF-SCOPE. An exact tier requires every opportunity to rank
applicants by appeal, and a graded tier admits near-vertical markets. On 30 30 held-out synthetic markets, the screen agrees with every pre-specified
regime verdict, with no observed false PASS. On 60 60 exactly vertical
markets, no bound is violated, and the probabilistic bound is informative in 69 % 69\% to 87 % 87\% of configurations. On 2700 2700 configurations from three
realistic markets, which do not reach the exact tier, no plug-in bound
expression is violated. A closed-form factorization stays within graded
scope in 90 % 90\% to 100 % 100\% of instances, whereas two-tower and graph neural
network encoders fall outside it in every instance. Architecture choice thus
appears to affect whether a post-hoc edit is admissible.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many machine learning systems make one-sided decisions, such as approving a loan or selecting an item to display. Two-sided matching systems instead allocate opportunities jointly across two populations. Examples include school and university admissions, residency matching, ride-sharing platforms, and freelance marketplaces. School choice and residency matching commonly use deferred acceptance. Under deferred acceptance, an agent’s outcome depends on the scores of all other agents. Raising one applicant’s score can trigger a chain of reassignments that displaces other applicants from their matches [ 23 ] . A small score change can therefore produce a large and discontinuous change in the final matching. Standard smoothness arguments do not directly apply to the effect of a model adjustment on such a mechanism. Consider a platform that scores applicants with a deployed model and allocates them through such a mechanism. Automated systems that decide access or admission to education are classified as high-risk under the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act [ 6 ] . In such settings, a regulator or an internal policy team may require a protected attribute, such as race or gender, to exert less influence on the matching. These requirements also change over time. In 2023, for example, the Supreme Court of the United States held that race-conscious admissions programs at two universities violated the Equal Protection Clause [ 26 ] . The platform could retrain the model after each change, but retraining is costly. Deep recommendation models are among the most compute-intensive training workloads in large production data centers [ 2 ] , and graph-based recommenders at web scale are trained on multi-GPU hardware over graphs with billions of nodes [ 31 ] . Repeated retraining may therefore be impractical, which motivates the following research question.

sections.heading: Research question
sections.text: Can the dependence of a deployed matching system on a protected attribute be reduced after deployment, without retraining, while providing a provable bound on the loss in match quality and a pre-deployment check that reports whether the bound applies? We address this question without differentiating the matching mechanism. We treat the mechanism as a black box, run it before and after a closed-form edit of the encoder output, and bound the resulting change in mean welfare. Because deferred acceptance is discontinuous in the scores, a bound of this kind requires structural assumptions on the market. The central problem is therefore to identify a market structure under which the edit has a bounded welfare cost, and to check that structure before deployment.

sections.heading: Contributions
sections.text: 1. We formulate four requirements for a post-hoc fairness intervention that leaves the encoder unchanged. A linear projection of the encoder output satisfies three of them by construction. The fourth is a provable bound on the loss in match quality. 2. For markets in which both sides share a ranking criterion before and after the edit, we prove a bound on the change in match quality that neither smooths nor approximates the matching mechanism. To our knowledge, this is the first such guarantee for a post-hoc edit in two-sided matching. An explicit form of the bound depends on quantities that can be estimated before deployment from the representations and a labeled validation set: the overlap between the removed information and agent merit, the alignment of the removed information with the ranking criterion, and the dispersion of merit among agents with equal appeal. 3. We derive a probabilistic refinement that replaces worst-case quantities with a data-dependent deviation term at a specified failure probability. 4. We combine the scope condition of the guarantees with an empirical welfare sweep in a pre-deployment screen that returns Pass , Kill , or Out-of-Scope according to predefined scope, gap-closure, and surplus-retention criteria. 5. We evaluate, on controlled and realistic markets, how the encoder architecture affects the scope conditions and the deployment verdicts. Section 2 positions the work in the literature. Section 3.1 formulates the problem and the intervention, and Section 3.2 develops the theoretical analysis. Section 3.3 presents the screening rule, and Section 4 reports the experiments. Section 5 interprets the findings and states the scope of the results, and Section 6 concludes.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Four lines of work address parts of the deployment problem considered here: concept erasure, post-processing fairness, in-processing fair ranking and recommendation, and fair matching mechanisms. Table 1 compares them on four properties of a deployable intervention: operation after training, retargeting to a new fairness objective without retraining, closed-form construction, and a bound on welfare cost. Classical two-sided matching theory, reviewed last, supplies the mechanism analysis rather than a competing intervention. Table 1 : Properties of representative approaches. The welfare guarantee of this work is conditional on vertical-market assumptions. Method Post-hoc Retargetable Closed-form Welfare Bound Concept erasure Yes Yes Partial No Post-processing fairness Yes Yes Partial No In-processing fair ranking/recommendation No No No No Fair matching mechanisms N/A N/A N/A No (mechanism only) This work Yes Yes Yes Yes (conditional) Concept erasure: Early methods removed a target attribute from static word embeddings by projecting out an estimated bias direction [ 4 ] . Later work introduced iterative nullspace projection [ 18 ] , adversarial linear erasure [ 19 ] , and closed-form projectors such as LEACE [ 3 ] . These methods prevent a linear classifier from recovering a concept from the representation. They operate post hoc and can be retargeted, and some admit closed-form solutions. Their guarantees concern the linear predictability of the attribute and the distortion of the representation. They do not bound the allocation that a discontinuous mechanism computes from all scores jointly. The projector analyzed here has the same structure as LEACE for a binary attribute. It removes the group mean-difference direction in whitened coordinates and maps the result back. It differs in whitening the pooled representations of both market sides and in allowing partial erasure. The contribution of this work is therefore not the projector itself but the analysis of its effect on the resulting allocation. Post-processing fairness: Post-processing methods adjust decisions or scores after training. Examples include equalized-odds post-processing [ 10 ] , its calibrated variant [ 17 ] , and reject-option classification [ 14 ] . Fair ranking methods such as FA*IR [ 32 ] and exposure-constrained rankings [ 24 ] similarly re-rank a given scored list. Like concept erasure, these methods are post hoc and can be reapplied to new targets. Their guarantees, however, concern individual predictions, aggregate classifier performance, or a single ranked list. Deferred acceptance processes all adjusted scores simultaneously, so a guarantee for independent decisions does not transfer to the induced matching. Representation neutralization [ 5 ] is the closest method in this group. It keeps the encoder fixed and retrains only the classification head on neutralized representations, so it also avoids retraining the encoder. It differs from the edit studied here in two respects. It retrains the head for each fairness target, and it addresses individual classification rather than a jointly computed allocation. In-processing fair ranking and recommendation: In-processing methods build fairness into the training objective. Early approaches learned representations that retained predictive information while obscuring group membership [ 33 ] . Later work added fairness regularizers to collaborative filtering [ 30 ] , decomposed embeddings into bias-aware and bias-free components for news recommendation [ 28 ] , and learned exposure-fair ranking policies [ 25 ] . These methods retrain the model when the fairness criterion changes. Filter-based methods [ 29 ] keep the base encoder fixed but train a separate filter for each fairness target. Neither class is retargetable without training, and neither provides a closed-form inference-time edit. When the protected attribute correlates with match quality, these methods also fix the accuracy-fairness tradeoff during training rather than measure it at inference time. Fair matching mechanisms: Fair matching methods change the allocation mechanism itself, through quotas, capacity constraints, or fair stable-matching procedures [ 13 , 16 , 9 ] . They impose distributional constraints on group representation directly. This work instead keeps the deployed mechanism fixed and edits only its inputs. The first three properties in Table 1 describe edits to the inputs of a fixed mechanism, so they are marked not applicable for these methods. The two approaches are complementary, and a platform could use both. Two-sided matching theory: The mechanism analysis builds on classical results on stability and deferred acceptance [ 8 ] , their application to school choice [ 1 ] , and the broader market design literature [ 22 ] . Stable assortative matching under vertical preferences is central to the theoretical framework. Recent work learns matching mechanisms that trade off stability and strategy-proofness [ 20 ] , whereas the mechanism here is given. To our knowledge, prior work has not connected assortative matching theory to post-hoc edits of trained representations or to welfare guarantees for such edits. Among the methods reviewed here, none combines post-hoc operation, retargetability, closed-form construction, and a welfare bound for the induced matching. The present framework provides all four properties for markets that satisfy explicit structural assumptions.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Two-sided matching systems
sections.text: A two-sided matching system contains two populations. Side 𝒜 \mathcal{A} contains applicants, such as users, students, or job seekers, while side ℬ \mathcal{B} contains opportunities, such as items, schools, or positions. A trained encoder E E maps each agent to a representation, where x a = E ⁡ ( a ) x_{a}=E(a) , x b = E ⁡ ( b ) x_{b}=E(b) , and x a , x b ∈ ℝ d x_{a},x_{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . A scorer assigns each pair the compatibility score s ⁡ ( a , b ) = ⟨ ϕ ⁡ ( x a ) , ψ ⁡ ( x b ) ⟩ s(a,b)=\langle\phi(x_{a}),\psi(x_{b})\rangle . In the preference model studied here, side ℬ \mathcal{B} ranks applicants by this score, while side 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ranks opportunities by their fixed quality q b q_{b} . An allocation mechanism ℳ \mathcal{M} maps the two sides’ rankings to a matching μ = ℳ ⁡ ( s , q ) \mu=\mathcal{M}(s,q) . Throughout this paper, ℳ \mathcal{M} is deferred acceptance. Side 𝒜 \mathcal{A} carries a protected attribute z ∈ { 0 , 1 } z\in\{0,1\} that may affect the scores and, consequently, the allocation. Only the ranking by side ℬ \mathcal{B} depends on the edit. The qualities of side ℬ \mathcal{B} are therefore fixed primitives, and the analysis of Section 3.2 attributes any welfare change to the movement of applicants along the quality ladder. Throughout, the market is balanced, one to one, and complete: | 𝒜 | = | ℬ | = n |\mathcal{A}|=|\mathcal{B}|=n , every agent ranks every agent on the other side, and no agent is left unmatched. Ties in the edited scores are broken by agent index, which fixes the matching uniquely when a projection creates exact ties.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Design requirements
sections.text: A post-hoc intervention on a deployed matcher should meet four deployment-oriented requirements, stated in Definition 1 . Definition 1 (Post-hoc fairness control with bounded cost) . An intervention on a trained matcher satisfies: (D1) It acts at inference time on the fixed encoder, without gradient updates to it. (D2) It is adjustable across fairness targets by changing few parameters, without retraining. (D3) It admits a closed form, recomputable cheaply when the attribute or population changes. (D4) It carries a bound on the match quality forfeited as a function of the intervention’s strength. Requirements D1–D3 distinguish post-hoc interventions from in-processing approaches. In-processing methods generally retrain the encoder when the protected attribute or fairness objective changes, which violates D1 and D2. They also provide no closed-form update for inexpensive recomputation, which violates D3. The projector introduced next satisfies D1–D3 by construction (Section 3.1.4 ). D4 instead requires a bound on the match quality forfeited as a function of edit strength. Construction alone cannot provide this bound because deferred acceptance is discontinuous in the scores. Without additional structure, a small input perturbation need not produce a small change in the matching. Establishing D4 is therefore the main theoretical problem. Section 3.2 establishes it for markets with a shared ranking criterion.

sections.heading: 3.1.5 Theoretical scope
sections.text: Because deferred acceptance is discontinuous in the scores (Section 3.1.2 ), the welfare analysis assumes a vertically ordered market in which both sides rank agents by a shared criterion. Under this structure, the stable matching is assortative, and the effect of the edit can be expressed as rank displacement. Markets with substantially idiosyncratic preferences fall outside this theoretical scope.

The fraction of score-matrix variance explained by the leading singular direction, which equals 1 1 when the score matrix is rank one, does not test Assumption 1 . For a bilinear score the matrix θ ​ q ⊤ \theta q^{\top} is rank one whatever the signs of θ \theta and q q , and a negative entry of q q reverses the ranking that the corresponding agent induces over the other side. sections.heading: 4.8 Comparison to prior post-hoc interventions
sections.text: We compare the proposed method with iterative nullspace projection [ 18 ] and three simplified reimplementations of prior approaches. The RLACE-style baseline alternates a linear adversary with an exponential-moving-average update of the erased direction rather than using the constrained minimax solver in [ 19 ] . Group score standardization rescales each group’s appeal scores to the pooled mean and standard deviation, following the general post-processing principle of [ 10 ] , without outcome labels. The reject-option-style baseline moves disadvantaged-group scores within a band around the pooled median halfway toward the advantaged-group mean, following [ 14 ] . All four baselines operate at inference time on a fixed encoder and use the same market, mechanism, and metrics. Tables 10 and 11 report the fraction of the group gap closed and the welfare retained relative to the uncorrected system. For the proposed method, the screening rule selects both γ \gamma and the verdict. We evaluate the LM-HB and HM-LB regimes of Section 4.1 , each with n = 400 n=400 agents per side and 30 30 seeds. Each baseline is evaluated at its standard full-correction operating point. The comparison therefore assesses the procedures as deployed, not interventions of equal strength. sections.heading: 5.1 Interpretation of the welfare bounds
sections.text: The two welfare guarantees serve distinct roles. Theorem 1 is deterministic under its stated assumptions. Theorem 2 replaces the outlier-dominated constant with a deviation term and a nonzero failure probability under the exchangeability assumption, which can yield a tighter finite-sample bound. At the evaluated scales, the plug-in constants place the deterministic right-hand side above the feasible welfare range. The probabilistic refinement is numerically informative for 68.7 % 68.7\% to 87.3 % 87.3\% of the configurations within the exact scope (Section 4.3 ) and for 38.5 % 38.5\% to 46.1 % 46.1\% of the nominally vertical configurations (Section 4.4 ). Bound magnitude is interpretable only jointly with the scope verdict. On the synthetic markets, mean right-hand side and mean tightness distinguish the NV regime from the two nominally vertical regimes, even where the binary informative criterion does not. On the realistic markets, magnitude tracks the market rather than the scope verdict (Section 4.7 ). A bound computed outside Assumption 1 carries no guarantee, whether it is large or small. Scope is therefore reported as a separate field, and magnitude serves as a continuous severity indicator only within scope.

sections.heading: 5.2 Screen availability as a model-selection criterion
sections.text: The three encoders represent common classes of production systems. A0 represents classical matrix-factorization recommenders and score-priority allocation systems, such as admissions based on standardized tests. A1 represents two-tower retrieval architectures that combine user and item towers at serving time. A2 represents graph-based recommenders that propagate information over an interaction graph. The closed-form factorization remains within graded scope for 90 % 90\% to 100 % 100\% of instances across the three markets, while both trained encoders are out of scope in every instance, despite using the same data, attribute, and target. These results suggest that a fairness audit may not transfer across architectures. Applying the screen to candidate representations before architecture selection would indicate whether the edit is admissible under the chosen empirical thresholds. This result can then be considered with predictive performance and latency.

sections.heading: 5.3 Entanglement as a diagnostic rather than a gate
sections.text: For the in-scope real-data cells, PASS rates are not monotonic in entanglement (Section 4.7 ). Proposition 1 bounds the welfare change at each edit strength γ \gamma , while Section 4.5 evaluates full erasure. The screen selects the smallest tested edit meeting both gap-closure and surplus-retention targets. Passing instances use partial edits that retain most of the assortative surplus. High entanglement therefore indicates that full erasure may be costly, but it does not imply that every gap-closing partial edit is costly. Proposition 1 also shows that entanglement alone does not determine the cost of an edit. The measurable shift scale δ γ \delta_{\gamma} in Equation ( 6 ) depends on c = | ⟨ W − 1 ​ u ^ , k ⟩ | c=|\langle W^{-1}\hat{u},k\rangle| and the perpendicular spread B ⟂ B_{\perp} , in addition to ent \mathrm{ent} . Unless representation spread is concentrated along the merit direction, entanglement alone does not determine the bound. The surplus sweep instead measures the realized cost of each candidate edit, and the verdict uses this measurement. For deployments that require full erasure rather than a target-driven partial edit, entanglement remains a directly relevant diagnostic.

sections.heading: 5.4 Scope and limitations
sections.text: The guarantees are market-design results based on order statistics, ranks, and a Lipschitz utility function. They are independent of the training loss, optimization procedure, and encoder construction. Their scope is limited to inference-time sensitivity: they neither smooth ℳ \mathcal{M} nor provide a surrogate gradient for end-to-end training through the mechanism. The locality argument in Lemma 2 applies to the rank-one perturbation in Equation ( 2 ) and does not directly cover an unconstrained multidirectional edit such as fine-tuning. The exact guarantees require a vertical market with a common ranking criterion before and after editing. Substantially idiosyncratic preferences, as in residency matching and freelance platforms, violate this structure. The analysis also assumes a balanced, one-to-one, complete market; capacities, unmatched agents, and incomplete preference lists are outside its scope. The graded tier admits near-vertical markets through a calibrated discordance threshold but has no corresponding theorem. In that tier, the screening verdict is supported by the empirical surplus-retention sweep, which re-solves the mechanism exactly. The intervention removes one linear mean-difference direction and does not eliminate nonlinear protected-attribute information or information distributed across several directions. The screening rule also requires estimates of utility and partner quality to evaluate surplus. Numerical use of the deterministic guarantee requires valid upper estimates of the population constants M M , Λ \Lambda , and f ¯ \bar{f} . The probabilistic refinement additionally requires exchangeability of quality-gap positions relative to the displacement pattern, which may fail for data-derived quality ladders. Within this scope, Theorems 1 and 2 bound the welfare effect of editing the output of a trained encoder, and Proposition 1 identifies the measurable quantities that control the cost. The screening rule connects these analytical conditions to the exact output of the allocation mechanism and separates exact-tier guarantees from graded empirical decisions.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and future work
sections.text: We studied whether an inference-time edit can attenuate the influence of a protected attribute on learned two-sided matching without retraining and with a cost that can be checked before deployment. For markets that remain vertically ordered before and after the edit, the welfare change caused by a closed-form projector is bounded by the edit-induced appeal shift and an explicit finite-sample and outlier remainder (Theorem 1 ). Under an additional exchangeability assumption, a probabilistic refinement improves finite-sample tightness by several orders of magnitude (Theorem 2 ). These results underlie a three-outcome screening rule. On 30 30 controlled synthetic markets, the screen agrees with every pre-specified regime verdict, with no observed false PASS. On exactly vertical synthetic markets, no evaluated bound is violated, and the probabilistic bound is informative in 69 % 69\% to 87 % 87\% of configurations. Across 270 270 instances from three realistic markets, the closed-form factorization remains within graded scope in at least 90 % 90\% of instances, whereas both trained encoders are out of scope in every instance. The realistic markets do not reach the exact tier, so their evaluations are stress tests. On such markets the screen supports model-selection and retraining audits under the graded criterion. Future work should first tighten the constants or develop high-probability surrogates for the supremum estimates in Proposition 1 . A second direction is to generalize Theorems 1 and 2 beyond rank-one edits and derive an analytical guarantee for the rank- ℓ \ell variant. A third direction is to identify weaker structural assumptions that support closed-form bounds in markets with idiosyncratic preferences, such as residency matching. Finally, the observed dependence on encoder architecture motivates training objectives that preserve a common ranking by construction. Such objectives could make screen compatibility a model-design constraint rather than only a post-training diagnostic.

Screening Post-Hoc Edits in Two-Sided Matching Markets Moirangthem Tiken Singh Email: tiken.m@dibru.ac.in Corresponding author: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Dibrugarh University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Dibrugarh University, Dibrugarh, Assam, India Rabinder Kumar Prasad Email: rkp@dibru.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Dibrugarh University Institute of Engineering and Technology, Dibrugarh University, Dibrugarh, Assam, India Abstract Two-sided matching systems, such as admissions pipelines, allocate opportunities jointly. Reducing a protected attribute’s influence usually requires encoder retraining. We study a closed-form linear projector that does this at inference time. For markets that stay vertically ordered before and after the edit, we bound the mean welfare change by the edit-induced appeal shift and an explicit remainder. A probabilistic refinement replaces worst-case constants with a data-dependent deviation term. A pre-deployment screen combines a verticality test with a welfare sweep and returns PASS, KILL, or OUT-OF-SCOPE. An exact tier requires every opportunity to rank applicants by appeal, and a graded tier admits near-vertical markets. On 30 30 held-out synthetic markets, the screen agrees with every pre-specified regime verdict, with no observed false PASS. On 60 60 exactly vertical markets, no bound is violated, and the probabilistic bound is informative in 69 % 69\% to 87 % 87\% of configurations. On 2700 2700 configurations from three realistic markets, which do not reach the exact tier, no plug-in bound expression is violated. A closed-form factorization stays within graded scope in 90 % 90\% to 100 % 100\% of instances, whereas two-tower and graph neural network encoders fall outside it in every instance. Architecture choice thus appears to affect whether a post-hoc edit is admissible. Keywords: Fairness in recommendation , Two-sided matching , Post-hoc intervention , Concept erasure , Welfare bound , Model selection 1 Introduction Many machine learning systems make one-sided decisions, such as approving a loan or selecting an item to display. Two-sided matching systems instead allocate opportunities jointly across two populations. Examples include school and university admissions, residency matching, ride-sharing platforms, and freelance marketplaces. School choice and residency matching commonly use deferred acceptance. Under deferred acceptance, an agent’s outcome depends on the scores of all other agents. Raising one applicant’s score can trigger a chain of reassignments that displaces other applicants from their matches [ 23 ] . A small score change can therefore produce a large and discontinuous change in the final matching. Standard smoothness arguments do not directly apply to the effect of a model adjustment on such a mechanism. Consider a platform that scores applicants with a deployed model and allocates them through such a mechanism. Automated systems that decide access or admission to education are classified as high-risk under the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act [ 6 ] . In such settings, a regulator or an internal policy team may require a protected attribute, such as race or gender, to exert less influence on the matching. These requirements also change over time. In 2023, for example, the Supreme Court of the United States held that race-conscious admissions programs at two universities violated the Equal Protection Clause [ 26 ] . The platform could retrain the model after each change, but retraining is costly. Deep recommendation models are among the most compute-intensive training workloads in large production data centers [ 2 ] , and graph-based recommenders at web scale are trained on multi-GPU hardware over graphs with billions of nodes [ 31 ] . Repeated retraining may therefore be impractical, which motivates the following research question. Research question Can the dependence of a deployed matching system on a protected attribute be reduced after deployment, without retraining, while providing a provable bound on the loss in match quality and a pre-deployment check that reports whether the bound applies? We address this question without differentiating the matching mechanism. We treat the mechanism as a black box, run it before and after a closed-form edit of the encoder output, and bound the resulting change in mean welfare. Because deferred acceptance is discontinuous in the scores, a bound of this kind requires structural assumptions on the market. The central problem is therefore to identify a market structure under which the edit has a bounded welfare cost, and to check that structure before deployment. Contributions 1. We formulate four requirements for a post-hoc fairness intervention that leaves the encoder unchanged. A linear projection of the encoder output satisfies three of them by construction. The fourth is a provable bound on the loss in match quality. 2. For markets in which both sides share a ranking criterion before and after the edit, we prove a bound on the change in match quality that neither smooths nor approximates the matching mechanism. To our knowledge, this is the first such guarantee for a post-hoc edit in two-sided matching. An explicit form of the bound depends on quantities that can be estimated before deployment from the representations and a labeled validation set: the overlap between the removed information and agent merit, the alignment of the removed information with the ranking criterion, and the dispersion of merit among agents with equal appeal. 3. We derive a probabilistic refinement that replaces worst-case quantities with a data-dependent deviation term at a specified failure probability. 4. We combine the scope condition of the guarantees with an empirical welfare sweep in a pre-deployment screen that returns Pass , Kill , or Out-of-Scope according to predefined scope, gap-closure, and surplus-retention criteria. 5. We evaluate, on controlled and realistic markets, how the encoder architecture affects the scope conditions and the deployment verdicts. Section 2 positions the work in the literature. Section 3.1 formulates the problem and the intervention, and Section 3.2 develops the theoretical analysis. Section 3.3 presents the screening rule, and Section 4 reports the experiments. Section 5 interprets the findings and states the scope of the results, and Section 6 concludes. 2 Related work Four lines of work address parts of the deployment problem considered here: concept erasure, post-processing fairness, in-processing fair ranking and recommendation, and fair matching mechanisms. Table 1 compares them on four properties of a deployable intervention: operation after training, retargeting to a new fairness objective without retraining, closed-form construction, and a bound on welfare cost. Classical two-sided matching theory, reviewed last, supplies the mechanism analysis rather than a competing intervention. Table 1 : Properties of representative approaches. The welfare guarantee of this work is conditional on vertical-market assumptions. Method Post-hoc Retargetable Closed-form Welfare Bound Concept erasure Yes Yes Partial No Post-processing fairness Yes Yes Partial No In-processing fair ranking/recommendation No No No No Fair matching mechanisms N/A N/A N/A No (mechanism only) This work Yes Yes Yes Yes (conditional) Concept erasure: Early methods removed a target attribute from static word embeddings by projecting out an estimated bias direction [ 4 ] . Later work introduced iterative nullspace projection [ 18 ] , adversarial linear erasure [ 19 ] , and closed-form projectors such as LEACE [ 3 ] . These methods prevent a linear classifier from recovering a concept from the representation. They operate post hoc and can be retargeted, and some admit closed-form solutions. Their guarantees concern the linear predictability of the attribute and the distortion of the representation. They do not bound the allocation that a discontinuous mechanism computes from all scores jointly. The projector analyzed here has the same structure as LEACE for a binary attribute. It removes the group mean-difference direction in whitened coordinates and maps the result back. It differs in whitening the pooled representations of both market sides and in allowing partial erasure. The contribution of this work is therefore not the projector itself but the analysis of its effect on the resulting allocation. Post-processing fairness: Post-processing methods adjust decisions or scores after training. Examples include equalized-odds post-processing [ 10 ] , its calibrated variant [ 17 ] , and reject-option classification [ 14 ] . Fair ranking methods such as FA*IR [ 32 ] and exposure-constrained rankings [ 24 ] similarly re-rank a given scored list. Like concept erasure, these methods are post hoc and can be reapplied to new targets. Their guarantees, however, concern individual predictions, aggregate classifier performance, or a single ranked list. Deferred acceptance processes all adjusted scores simultaneously, so a guarantee for independent decisions does not transfer to the induced matching. Representation neutralization [ 5 ] is the closest method in this group. It keeps the encoder fixed and retrains only the classification head on neutralized representations, so it also avoids retraining the encoder. It differs from the edit studied here in two respects. It retrains the head for each fairness target, and it addresses individual classification rather than a jointly computed allocation. In-processing fair ranking and recommendation: In-processing methods build fairness into the training objective. Early approaches learned representations that retained predictive information while obscuring group membership [ 33 ] . Later work added fairness regularizers to collaborative filtering [ 30 ] , decomposed embeddings into bias-aware and bias-free components for news recommendation [ 28 ] , and learned exposure-fair ranking policies [ 25 ] . These methods retrain the model when the fairness criterion changes. Filter-based methods [ 29 ] keep the base encoder fixed but train a separate filter for each fairness target. Neither class is retargetable without training, and neither provides a closed-form inference-time edit. When the protected attribute correlates with match quality, these methods also fix the accuracy-fairness tradeoff during training rather than measure it at inference time. Fair matching mechanisms: Fair matching methods change the allocation mechanism itself, through quotas, capacity constraints, or fair stable-matching procedures [ 13 , 16 , 9 ] . They impose distributional constraints on group representation directly. This work instead keeps the deployed mechanism fixed and edits only its inputs. The first three properties in Table 1 describe edits to the inputs of a fixed mechanism, so they are marked not applicable for these methods. The two approaches are complementary, and a platform could use both. Two-sided matching theory: The mechanism analysis builds on classical results on stability and deferred acceptance [ 8 ] , their application to school choice [ 1 ] , and the broader market design literature [ 22 ] . Stable assortative matching under vertical preferences is central to the theoretical framework. Recent work learns matching mechanisms that trade off stability and strategy-proofness [ 20 ] , whereas the mechanism here is given. To our knowledge, prior work has not connected assortative matching theory to post-hoc edits of trained representations or to welfare guarantees for such edits. Among the methods reviewed here, none combines post-hoc operation, retargetability, closed-form construction, and a welfare bound for the induced matching.
